text.en: Imagine you have tried something many times and failed every time. Would you give up? This old poem is about a king who nearly did, until a tiny spider showed him what trying again really means.

The chapter begins by asking who inspires you to do your best. You then look at six pictures and say what we can learn from them, such as patience, hard work and never giving up.
King Bruce of Scotland lies down alone and sad. Though he is a king and wears a crown, his heart is sinking, because he has tried again and again to do a great deed that would make his people glad, and has failed. In low despair he thinks aloud that he will give it all up. At that moment a spider drops down on a fine, silky thread. The king stops thinking and watches what it will do. The spider hangs by a very thin rope a long way below the ceiling, and Bruce cannot guess how it will reach its web. The spider climbs, inch by inch, but tumbles down every time. It tries nine times in all. On each fall the king feels anxious, wondering whether it will win or lose. At last the spider reaches its cobweb home. Bruce says the spider has conquered, and so will he. Inspired by its determination, he decides to try once more, and this time he succeeds.
The poem is written in a narrative style, because it tells a story with a beginning, a middle and an end, and it has a character, a problem and a result. The central idea is perseverance: if we keep trying and do not give up, failure becomes a stepping stone to success. The word tried is repeated in tried and tried, and steadily is repeated, and up, up, to show how long, slow and steady the effort was. Repetition stresses the spider's effort.
The rhyme scheme is ABAB, so alternate lines rhyme, as in down, think, crown, sink. Bravo is an interjection, a word that shows a sudden feeling. The poet uses 'twas and 'tis, which are short forms of it was and it is, to keep the rhythm of the verse. A metaphor is an implied comparison without like or as. The spider's climbing is a picture of Bruce's own struggle, and this strengthens the message of perseverance. In the exercise, he ran as fast as a cheetah, the night was as dark as coal, he sang like an angel, the baby slept like a log and her smile was as bright as the sun are similes. The world is a stage, her voice was music to his ears, the classroom was a zoo and the lake was a mirror are metaphors. To change a simile into a metaphor, drop like or as, for example knowledge is a spreading branch of a mighty tree. To change a metaphor into a simile, add like or as, for example his courage was like a beacon.
In flung himself down in low despair, the word low shows how deep his sadness was, and flung shows the physical expression of his mood. Pondered means thought. Silken, filmy clue describes a very delicate, soft thread. Toil means to work very hard, and the line toil: hard is like roll: tumble, since tumble is a way of rolling. Ah me shows a sense of stress, because the king anxiously waits. We relate to it because everyone has felt anxious when failing and trying again. The spider shows determination, patience and courage.
The opposites are up and down, fast and slow, glad and sad, win and lose, succeed and fail. Endeavour means an attempt to do something new or difficult, toil means to work very hard for a long time, strive means to try very hard, and braced means prepared for something difficult. Words that show distance in the poem include a long way up, inch by inch, higher and higher and half-yard higher. Remoteness and light year suggest far, and proximity suggests near. The tongue twister is the line about a delicate thread it had to tread. Say it five or six times and then make your own tongue twisters. In the listening story about an ant, the ant is known for determination. Let your teacher read the transcript and check your guesses. For speaking, tell about a time you nearly gave up and a person or thing inspired you. Introduce the situation, describe the challenge, say how you felt and what helped, and end with what you learned.

problem.en: Mark each as simile or metaphor: (a) He sang like an angel. (b) The classroom was a zoo.

text.en: Look for like or as.

why.en: Sentence (a) has like, so it is a simile.

text.en: Sentence (b) says one thing is another.

problem.en: Turn the simile into a metaphor: her thoughts were like butterflies.

text.en: Remove like.
Check the meaning stays.

prompt.en: Explain how the spider changes King Bruce and what the poem teaches.

requiredIdeas.en: The king was sad and ready to give up.
He watched a spider fall and climb again nine times.
He tried once more and succeeded, so the poem teaches perseverance.

commonMisconceptions.en: The king gave up in the end.
The spider reached its web on the first attempt.

points.en: King Bruce was ready to give up until he watched a spider try again and again.
The spider reached its web after nine tries.
The poem is a narrative with the central idea of perseverance.
Similes use like or as, metaphors do not.
